passages.title: Reading Passage 1 · A Bank for the World's Seeds
passages.note: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1.
paras: On a remote Arctic island, about thirteen hundred kilometres from the North Pole, a narrow concrete entrance leads into the side of a mountain. Behind it, at the end of a tunnel more than one hundred metres long, lies one of the most unusual stores in the world. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault does not contain gold or important documents, but more than a million packets of seeds, collected from almost every country on Earth. Its purpose is simple: to make sure that the world's food crops can be saved if disaster strikes.

The idea of storing seeds for the future is not new. In the 1920s, the Russian scientist Nikolai Vavilov travelled across five continents collecting seeds and established one of the first large seed collections in what is now St Petersburg. Today there are around seventeen hundred seed banks around the world, run by governments, universities and research organisations. They allow scientists and farmers to grow varieties of crops that might otherwise have disappeared, and to use their genes to breed new varieties that are able to resist diseases or survive in difficult conditions.

However, many of these seed banks are vulnerable. Some have been damaged by war, as happened to national collections in Afghanistan and Iraq. Others have suffered from natural disasters: in 2006, a typhoon flooded the national seed bank of the Philippines. Even in peaceful countries, collections can be lost because of power cuts, equipment failures or simple lack of money. The Svalbard vault was designed as a back-up for these collections, a place where copies of their seeds would be kept safe whatever happened elsewhere.

The location was chosen with great care. Svalbard is politically stable, and the vault is far enough above sea level, at around one hundred and thirty metres, to remain dry even if the polar ice caps melt completely. Most importantly, the surrounding rock is permafrost, ground that remains frozen all year round. The seeds are stored at minus eighteen degrees Celsius, the temperature at which they can survive for decades or even centuries, and electric cooling systems are used to maintain this. If the electricity were to fail, however, the natural cold of the mountain would keep the seeds frozen for many years.

The vault opened in February 2008. It was paid for by the Norwegian government, which also owns the building, but the seeds remain the property of the organisations that deposit them. In this way, the vault operates rather like a safe deposit box at a bank: Norway looks after the boxes but cannot open them, and only the original depositor can request that its seeds be returned. Deposits are free of charge, while the running costs are shared between Norway and an international organisation called the Crop Trust.

The vault has three storage halls, each capable of holding one and a half million seed samples, so the total capacity is four and a half million. At present only one hall is in use. Each sample contains on average about five hundred seeds, sealed in specially made foil packets that keep out moisture. The most common crops in the vault are rice, wheat and barley, but it also holds seeds of hundreds of less familiar plants, from wild relatives of crops to traditional varieties grown by a single community.

For several years the vault was regarded as an insurance policy that would probably never be needed. That changed in 2015, when an important research centre based in Aleppo, Syria, was forced to move because of the war in that country. The centre, which had specialised in crops suited to dry regions, requested the return of some of the copies of its seeds that it had deposited at Svalbard. Using these seeds, it was able to rebuild its collection in new facilities in Lebanon and Morocco, and later sent fresh copies back to the vault. It remains the only withdrawal in the vault's history so far.

The vault has not been entirely free of problems. In 2016, unusually warm temperatures caused melting snow to enter the entrance tunnel. No seeds were damaged, since the water froze long before it reached the storage halls, but the incident attracted worldwide attention and led to a major upgrade of the building, including a new waterproof entrance tunnel and a separate building for the electrical equipment, which produces heat. The work was completed in 2019.

Some critics argue that storing seeds in a freezer is not enough. Crops in fields continue to change over time as they adapt to new pests and a changing climate, while frozen seeds remain the same. For this reason, many experts believe that seed banks should be seen as only one part of the solution, alongside support for farmers who continue to grow and exchange traditional varieties. Nevertheless, as climate change threatens harvests in many parts of the world, few would argue that the vault on Svalbard is unnecessary.

passages.title: Reading Passage 2 · Setting Rivers Free
passages.note: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2.
paras: A  Across Europe, rivers have been blocked for centuries. Mills, canals, flood defences and hydroelectric power stations have all required barriers, and a recent survey counted more than one million of them on the continent's rivers, an average of almost one barrier for every kilometre. Many are small weirs, little more than a metre high, built for purposes that no longer exist. Yet even these can prevent fish from moving upstream to breed, and they can change the way sediment such as sand and gravel moves along a river.

B  In recent years, a movement to remove unnecessary barriers has gained momentum. In 2023 alone, more than four hundred and eighty were taken down in European countries, with Spain, France and Sweden among the most active. The European Union has set a target of restoring at least twenty-five thousand kilometres of free-flowing rivers by 2030. Supporters argue that removing obsolete barriers is one of the quickest and cheapest ways to improve the health of a river, since nature often recovers by itself once the obstacle has gone.

C  The best-known example of dam removal, however, comes from North America. On the Elwha River in the state of Washington, two large dams built in the early twentieth century were removed between 2011 and 2014, at the time the largest dam removal project in history. Before the dams were built, the river had been famous for its salmon, which travelled up the river each year to breed. Within a few years of removal, salmon had returned to parts of the river they had not reached for a century, and the sediment released from behind the dams had rebuilt a beach at the river mouth.

D  The benefits are not limited to fish. According to the ecologist Dr Hanna Lindqvist, a free-flowing river supports a far wider range of life, from insects to birds. 'When water moves freely, it creates a variety of habitats: fast and slow sections, deep pools, gravel banks,' she explains. 'A reservoir behind a dam is basically one habitat, and a fairly poor one.' Rivers without barriers may also cope better with rising temperatures, since fish can move upstream to cooler water in summer.

E  Not everyone is enthusiastic. Some local residents value the ponds and lakes created by old dams, which may be popular for fishing or simply admired as part of the landscape. Historians have also objected to the loss of mills and weirs that are part of a region's industrial heritage. Professor Marc Duval, who studies historic waterways, argues that each case should be judged individually. 'We should not remove a two-hundred-year-old structure just because it is old,' he says. 'In some cases, a fish pass can be added, allowing fish to swim around the barrier while keeping the structure in place.'

F  There are also practical risks. When a dam is removed, large quantities of sediment that have built up behind it may be released at once, which can harm fish and make the water unsuitable for drinking until it settles. In some cases, the sediment contains pollution from former industries. Engineer Sofia Marques, who has worked on several removal projects in Portugal, says careful planning is essential. 'The most important stage is the investigation beforehand,' she says. 'We test the sediment and decide whether it can be released gradually or needs to be removed by machines first.'

G  Large hydroelectric dams, which provide renewable energy, are a different matter, and very few people are suggesting that these should be removed. The focus is on the many thousands of small barriers that no longer serve any purpose. According to the river campaigner Tom Ashby, the biggest challenge is often not technical but administrative. 'In many cases, nobody knows who owns a particular weir,' he says. 'Before you can remove it, you have to find the owner, and that can take years.'

passages.title: Reading Passage 3 · The Power of Expectation
passages.note: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3.
paras: During the Second World War, an American doctor called Henry Beecher was working with injured soldiers in Italy when supplies of the painkiller morphine ran low. According to a story that has been retold many times, a nurse injected a wounded soldier with salt water but told him it was morphine. To Beecher's surprise, the soldier's pain appeared to decrease. After the war, Beecher went on to study the phenomenon systematically, and in 1955 he published an influential paper claiming that around a third of patients improved when given treatments with no active ingredient. Such treatments became known as placebos, from a Latin word meaning 'I shall please'.

Beecher's figure is no longer accepted. Later researchers pointed out that many patients in his studies would probably have improved anyway, simply because many illnesses get better on their own, and because people tend to seek treatment when their symptoms are at their worst. Nevertheless, the basic idea that a patient's beliefs can affect their symptoms has been confirmed in many carefully controlled experiments. It is the reason why new drugs are tested against placebos: a drug is only considered effective if it works better than an identical-looking pill containing no medicine.

The placebo effect appears to be strongest for symptoms that the brain plays a large part in producing, such as pain, nausea and tiredness. Brain-imaging studies have shown that when people who have been given a placebo painkiller expect relief, their brains release natural pain-reducing chemicals called endorphins. In one experiment, when participants were secretly given a drug that blocks the effect of endorphins, the placebo stopped working. This suggests that the effect is not simply a matter of patients imagining that they feel better or trying to please their doctor, but involves real physical changes.

Remarkably, the details of a placebo make a difference. Studies have found that two placebo pills are more effective than one, that injections tend to be more effective than pills, and that capsules are often more effective than tablets. Colour matters too: in several studies, blue pills were found to be more calming than red ones. Even price can be important. In one experiment, volunteers who were told that a placebo painkiller cost two and a half dollars reported more pain relief than those who were told it had been reduced to ten cents.

Perhaps the most surprising finding is that placebos can work even when patients know they are taking them. In a study led by Ted Kaptchuk at Harvard University, patients with a painful digestive condition were given pills and told honestly that they contained no medicine, but that placebos had been shown to help some people. After three weeks, these patients reported significantly greater improvement than a group who received no pills at all. Similar results have since been reported for back pain and tiredness, although the studies have generally been small.

There is also a negative side. If positive expectations can make people feel better, negative expectations can make them feel worse. This is known as the nocebo effect. In drug trials, many patients who receive a placebo report side effects such as headaches or dizziness, often the same side effects that they were warned about when they agreed to take part. Some researchers believe the nocebo effect helps to explain why a significant number of people stop taking useful medicines, having read long lists of possible side effects.

In my view, these findings raise difficult questions for doctors. Giving patients a placebo while telling them it is a real drug involves deception, which most medical organisations regard as unacceptable. However, the research suggests that doctors may be able to use the placebo effect honestly, for example by speaking positively and confidently about a treatment, or by spending more time with patients. Studies have found that a warm and attentive manner can itself reduce symptoms, which may partly explain why some patients report benefits from alternative therapies whose ingredients have no proven effect.

It is important, however, not to exaggerate what placebos can do. There is no good evidence that they can shrink tumours, cure infections or repair broken bones. Their effects are largely limited to how patients feel, rather than to the underlying disease. Used wisely, the placebo effect is not a replacement for medicine, but a reminder that the way treatment is given can matter almost as much as the treatment itself.
